en: Netti 5.
Origin of Methods.
Therein, what is the origin of methods?
No prior limit is discerned for ignorance (*avijjā*) and the craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*). In this regard, there is the hindrance of ignorance and the fetter of craving.
Beings hindered by ignorance and bound by ignorance wander about on the side of ignorance; they are called those of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhi-carita*).
Beings fettered by craving and bound by craving wander about on the side of craving; they are called those of craving temperament (*taṇhā-carita*).
Those of speculative temperament who have gone forth outside this [teaching] dwell devoted to the practice of self-mortification.
Those of craving-temperament who have gone forth outside this [teaching] dwell devoted to the pursuit of sensual pleasure among sense-desires.

What is the reason why those of speculative temperament who have gone forth outside this [teaching] dwell devoted to the practice of self-mortification, while those of craving-temperament who have gone forth outside this [teaching] dwell devoted to the pursuit of sensual pleasure among sense-desires?
Outside of this, there is no defining of truth; how then could there be the proclamation of the Four Truths, skill in serenity and insight, or the attainment of the bliss of peace?
Not having directly known the bliss of peace, those whose minds are perverted have said: "There is no happiness through happiness; happiness must indeed be attained through suffering.
He who indulges in sensual pleasures increases the world; he who increases the world generates much merit.

Having such perceptions and such views, longing for happiness amidst suffering, they dwell perceiving merit in sensual pleasures, devoted both to the pursuit of self-mortification and to the pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasure.
Through that very ignorance, they increase their disease, they increase their abscess, they increase their arrow; pierced by the arrow, oppressed by the abscess, and struck down by disease.
In the realms of hell-beings, animals, ghosts, and asuras, they repeatedly sink and surface, experiencing being cast up and cast down;
they find no remedy for the diseases, boils, and thorns [of suffering].
In this context, devotion to self-mortification and devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasures are defilements, while serenity and insight are purification.
Devotion to self-mortification and devotion to sensual pleasures are a disease; serenity and insight are the medicine that eliminates the disease.
Devotion to self-mortification and devotion to sensual pleasures are a tumor; serenity and insight are the medicine that eliminates the tumor.
Devotion to self-mortification and devotion to sensual pleasures are a dart; serenity and insight are the medicine for extracting the dart.

In this context, defilement is suffering; attachment to that is craving, which is the origin; the cessation of craving is the cessation of suffering; and serenity and insight are the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—these are the four truths.
Suffering is to be fully understood, the origin is to be abandoned, the path is to be developed, and cessation is to be realized.
In this regard, those of a speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) approach form as a self.
Feeling … perception … volitional formations … [and so on] … consciousness.
They approach consciousness as self.
Those of craving-temperament approach a self possessed of form;
or they approach form in the self, or a self in form.
One possessing feeling … pe … one possessing perception … one possessing volitional formations …
They approach a self possessed of consciousness, or consciousness in the self, or a self in consciousness; this is called the embodiment-view with twenty bases.

Its opposite is supramundane right view; following upon it are right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this is the Noble Eightfold Path.
These are the three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.
The aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration are serenity; the aggregate of wisdom is insight.

Therein, the personhood-aggregate (sakkāya) is suffering, the origin of the personhood-aggregate is the origin of suffering, the cessation of the personhood-aggregate is the cessation of suffering, and the noble eightfold path is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—these are the four truths.
Suffering is to be fully understood, its origin is to be abandoned, the path is to be developed, and cessation is to be realized.
In that regard, those who approach form as self,
[and] feeling … perception … [and so on].
They approach volitional formations … consciousness as self.
These are called "annihilationists."
Those who approach a self as possessing form, or form as being in the self, or the self as being in form;
those who [approach] a self as possessing feeling... [and so on].
Those who approach a self as possessing perception... those who approach a self as possessing volitional formations...
or those who approach a self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness in the self, or a self in consciousness.
These are called "eternalists. In this context, both the doctrines of annihilationism and eternalism are extremes; this is the occurrence of saṃsāra.
Its opposite is the middle way, the Noble Eightfold Path; this is the cessation of saṃsāra.

Therein, occurrence is suffering (dukkha), attachment to it is craving (taṇhā) as its origin (samudaya), the cessation of craving is the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodha), and the Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā). These are the Four Truths.
Suffering is to be fully understood; the origin is to be abandoned; the path is to be developed; cessation is to be realized.
In this regard, annihilationism and eternalism consist, in brief, of the twenty-based personality view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), and in detail, of the sixty-two types of views.
Their opposites are the forty-three factors conducive to enlightenment, the eight liberations, and the ten kasiṇa bases.
The sixty-two types of views are the net of delusion, proceeding without beginning or end.
The forty-three factors conducive to enlightenment are the diamond of knowledge, which shatters the net of delusion.

In this context, "delusion" is ignorance (*avijjā*), and the "net" is craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*); therefore it is said: "A prior limit is not discerned of ignorance and craving for existence."
In this regard, one of speculative temperament who has gone forth in this teaching becomes one whose conduct is continuous with effacement and who possesses intense reverence for effacement.
One of craving temperament who has gone forth in this teaching becomes one whose conduct is continuous with the training and who possesses intense reverence for the training.
One of speculative temperament who enters upon the certainty of rightness becomes a follower of the Dhamma.

One of craving-temperament, entering the fixed course of rightness, becomes a follower by faith; one of view-temperament issues forth by the pleasant way with either sluggish or swift direct knowledge.
One of craving-temperament issues forth by the painful way with either sluggish or swift direct knowledge.
In this regard, what is the reason that one of craving-temperament issues forth by the painful way with either sluggish or swift direct knowledge?
And he does not depart; for his sensual desires remain unrenounced, and being separated from sensual desires, he relinquishes them with difficulty and understands the Dhamma slowly.
But as for this one who is of a speculative temperament, from the very beginning he is without interest in sensual desires.
Thus, when being examined from that point, he quickly relinquishes [the defilement] and quickly understands the Dhamma.
The painful way of practice is twofold: with sluggish direct knowledge and with swift direct knowledge.
The pleasant way of practice is also twofold: with sluggish direct knowledge and with swift direct knowledge.
Beings are also of two kinds: those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties.
Those with dull faculties relinquish slowly and slowly comprehend the Dhamma;
those with sharp faculties relinquish quickly and quickly comprehend the Dhamma. These are the four modes of practice.
For whoever have crossed over, are crossing over, or will cross over, they do so by means of these very four ways.
Thus the Noble Ones prescribe the fourfold path for the purpose of turning back craving—the delight that is indulged in by ignorant people, beloved by fools, and dwelling in passion.
This is called the plane of the method of the "turning-back of delight" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*); therefore he said: "Craving and ignorance [are overcome] by tranquility."
For among the explanations, those that are wholesome and unwholesome should be examined in two ways:
as following the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and as following the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
"The cycle" (*vaṭṭa*) refers to saṃsāra.
Turning away is Nibbāna.
Karma and the defilements are the cause of saṃsāra.
Therein, karma should be demonstrated as both volition and mental factors.
How is that to be understood?
By way of accumulation, all defilements are to be demonstrated through the four perversions.
Where are they to be seen?
In the heap of defilements consisting of ten bases.
What are the ten bases?

The four nutriments, the four perversions, the four clingings, the four yokes, the four ties, the four taints, the four floods, the four arrows, the four stations of consciousness, and the four ways of going to a bad destination.
In the first nutriment is the first perversion; in the second nutriment is the second perversion; in the third nutriment is the third perversion; in the fourth nutriment is the fourth perversion.
In the first perversion is the first clinging; in the second perversion is the second clinging; in the third perversion is the third clinging; in the fourth perversion is the fourth clinging.
In the first clinging there is the first bond; in the second clinging there is the second bond; in the third clinging there is the third bond; in the fourth clinging there is the fourth bond.
In the first bond there is the first tie; in the second bond there is the second tie; in the third bond there is the third tie; in the fourth bond there is the fourth tie.
In the first tie there is the first taint; in the second tie there is the second taint; in the third tie there is the third taint; in the fourth tie there is the fourth taint.
In the first influx is the first flood; in the second influx is the second flood; in the third influx is the third flood; in the fourth influx is the fourth flood.
In the first flood is the first dart; in the second flood is the second dart; in the third flood is the third dart; in the fourth flood is the fourth dart.

In the first dart is the first station of consciousness; in the second dart is the second station of consciousness; in the third dart is the third station of consciousness; in the fourth dart is the fourth station of consciousness.
In the first station of consciousness, there is the first going on a bad way; in the second station of consciousness, the second going on a bad way;
in the third station of consciousness, the third going on a bad way; and in the fourth station of consciousness, the fourth going on a bad way.
Therein, edible food as nutriment and contact as nutriment are the defilements of a person of craving-disposition.
Mental volition as nutriment and consciousness as nutriment are the defilements of a person of view-disposition.
Therein, the perversion that takes the foul to be beautiful and the perversion that takes suffering to be pleasure are the defilements of a person of craving-disposition.

The perversion that takes what is impermanent to be permanent, and the perversion that takes what is non-self to be self—these are the defilements of a person of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*).
Among these, sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*) and existence-clinging (*bhavupādāna*) are the defilements of a person of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*);
while view-clinging (*diṭṭhupādāna*) and self-theory clinging (*attavādupādāna*) are the defilements of a person of speculative temperament.
In this regard, the yoke of sensual desire and the yoke of existence are the defilements of a person of craving-temperament.
The yoke of views and the yoke of ignorance are the defilements of a person of view-temperament.
Furthermore, the bodily tie of covetousness and the bodily tie of ill will are the defilements of a person of craving-temperament.
The bodily tie of misapprehension and the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence to "this alone is the truth" are the defilements of a person of speculative temperament.
Among these, the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence are the defilements of a person of craving temperament.
The taint of views and the taint of ignorance are the defilements of a person of speculative temperament.
In this regard, the flood of sensual desire and the flood of existence are the defilements of a person of craving-temperament.
The flood of views and the flood of ignorance are the defilements of a person of view-temperament.
In this regard, the dart of lust and the dart of hatred are the defilements of a person of craving-temperament.
The barb of conceit and the barb of delusion—these are the defilements of a person of speculative temperament.
Therein, the station of consciousness associated with form and the station of consciousness associated with feeling—these are the defilements of a person of craving temperament.
The station of consciousness associated with perception and the station of consciousness associated with mental formations—these are the defilements of a person of speculative temperament.
In this context, going astray through desire and going astray through hatred are the defilements of a person of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*).
Going astray through fear and going astray through delusion are the defilements of a person of view-temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*).
In this regard, regarding edible food, there is the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the ugly; regarding contact as food, there is the perversion of perceiving pleasure in the painful.

Regarding the perversions: there is the perversion of perceiving "the permanent in the impermanent" in relation to the nutriment of consciousness; there is the perversion of perceiving "self in the non-self" in relation to the nutriment of mental volition.
One established in the first perversion clings to sensual pleasures; this is called clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
One established in the second perversion clings to future existence; this is called clinging to existence (*bhavupādāna*).
Established in the third perversion, one clings to a view that delights in saṃsāra; this is called clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna).
Established in the fourth perversion, one clings to a self as being constructible; this is called clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna).
Through clinging to sensual pleasures, one is bound by sensual pleasures; this is called the yoke of sensual pleasure (kāmayoga).
Through the clinging to existence, one is bound to existence; this is called the yoke of existence.
Through the clinging to views, one is bound to evil views; this is called the yoke of views.
Through the clinging to a doctrine of self, one is bound to ignorance; this is called the yoke of ignorance.
One established in the first bond ties the body with covetousness; this is called the bodily bond of covetousness.
One established in the second bond ties the body with ill will; this is called the bodily bond of ill will.
One established in the third bond ties the body with dogmatic misapprehension; this is called the bodily bond of dogmatic misapprehension.
One established in the fourth bond (yoga) binds the body through the insistence that "this alone is the truth"; this is called the bodily bond of the insistence that "this alone is the truth.
Because one is thus bound, the defilements flow out.
And from what is it said that they "flow out"?
Either by way of underlying tendency (*anusaya*) or by way of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).

In this context, through the bodily tie of covetousness, there is the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*); through the bodily tie of ill will, the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*); through the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence, the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*); and through the bodily tie of insistence on "this alone is the truth," the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
When these four taints of his have reached full development, they become floods (*ogha*).
Thus, from the expansion of the taints comes the expansion of the floods.

Therein, through the taint of sensual desire there is the flood of sensual desire; through the taint of existence there is the flood of existence; through the taint of views there is the flood of views; and through the taint of ignorance there is the flood of ignorance.
These four floods of his, accompanied by underlying tendencies and having entered into his inclination, remain striking against his heart; therefore they are called "arrows."

In this context, by the flood of sensual desire there is the dart of lust; by the flood of existence there is the dart of hatred; by the flood of views there is the dart of conceit; and by the flood of ignorance there is the dart of delusion.
Consciousness, gripped by these four darts, becomes established upon four things: upon form, feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Therein, by means of consciousness that is moistened with delight through the dart of lust, there is the station of consciousness that has reached form; by the dart of hatred... [and so on].
The station of consciousness associated with feeling is a station of consciousness moistened by the sprinkling of delight;

the station of consciousness associated with perception is a station of consciousness moistened by the sprinkling of delight; the station of consciousness associated with mental formations is a station of consciousness moistened by the sprinkling of delight, [moistened] by the dart of delusion.
Consciousness, being propped up by these four stations of consciousness, goes astray through four things: through desire, through hatred, through fear, and through delusion.
Therein, through lust one goes to a wrong course out of desire; through hatred one goes to a wrong course out of hatred; through fear one goes to a wrong course out of fear;

through delusion one goes to a wrong course out of delusion. Thus, both that karma and these defilements are the cause of saṃsāra. In this way, all defilements are to be demonstrated by means of the four perversions (*vipallāsa*).
Therein, these are the four directions: edible food is the perversion of "the beautiful in the ugly," which is sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*).
The bond of sensual desire, the bodily tie of covetousness, the taint of sensual desire, the flood of sensual desire, the dart of lust, the station of consciousness that has reached form,
going on a wrong path through zeal— this is the first direction. Contact as nutriment,

the perversion of seeing pleasure in what is suffering, clinging to existence, the bond of existence, the bodily tie of ill will, the taint of existence, the flood of existence, the dart of hatred, the station of consciousness that has reached feeling, going on a wrong path through hatred— this is the second direction.

The nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*) is the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent; it is the clinging to views, the bond of views, the bodily tie of misapprehension, the taint of views, the flood of views, the dart of conceit, the station of consciousness associated with perception, and the going to a bad destination through fear—this is the third direction.
The nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*) is the perversion of perceiving what is non-self as self;

it is the clinging to the doctrine of self, the bond of ignorance, the bodily tie of insistence on "this alone is the truth," the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the dart of delusion, the station of consciousness associated with formations, and the going to a bad destination through delusion—this is the fourth direction.

In this regard, that which is edible food and the perversion that perceives "the beautiful in the ugly"— namely, clinging to sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasures, the bodily tie of covetousness,
the taint of sensual pleasures, the flood of sensual pleasures, the sting of lust, the station of consciousness associated with form, and going on a wrong path through desire—
these ten suttas have one meaning; only the phrasing is different.
These are the defilements of a person of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).
Among them, there is contact as nutriment, the perversion that "there is pleasure in what is suffering," the clinging to existence (*bhavupādāna*),

the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*), the bodily tie of ill-will (*byāpādakāyagantha*), the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), the flood of existence (*bhavogha*), the dart of hatred (*dosasalla*), and the station of consciousness associated with feeling that leads to hatred.
"Going on a wrong course": these ten suttas have one meaning; only the phrasing is different. These are the defilements of a person of a temperament characterized by vice.

In this context, that which is the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*), the perversion that takes "the impermanent as permanent," the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), and the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*)—[these are included therein].

The bodily tie of misapprehension, the taint of views, the flood of views, the dart of conceit, the station of consciousness accompanied by perception, and going to a bad destination out of fear—these ten suttas have one meaning; only the phrasing is different.
These are the imperfections of one of dull temperament who is dominated by views.
In this regard, the nutriment of mental volition, the perversion that takes what is non-self as self, the clinging to a doctrine of self, the bond of ignorance,
the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence to "this is the truth," the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the dart of delusion, the station of consciousness that enters into formations,
and the going on a wrong path due to delusion— these ten suttas have one meaning; only the phrasing is different.
These are the defilements of one whose temperament is dominated by views and who is exalted.
Therein, both the nutriment of physical food and the nutriment of contact reach full understanding through the door of liberation that is the wishless;
the nutriment of consciousness through emptiness; and the nutriment of mental volition through the signless. Therein, whatever...
The perversion that perceives the foul as beautiful, and the perversion that perceives suffering as pleasure—
these are abandoned and brought to an end by the door of liberation that is the wishless (*appaṇihita*).
The perversion that perceives the impermanent as permanent is abandoned by emptiness (*suññatā*), and the perversion that perceives the non-self as self is abandoned by the signless (*animitta*).
Therein, clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) and clinging to existence (*bhavupādāna*) are abandoned by means of the door of liberation that is wishless (*appaṇihita*).
Clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) is abandoned by means of emptiness (*suññatā*), and clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*) is abandoned by means of the signless (*animitta*).

Therein, the yoke of sensual pleasure (*kāmayoga*) and the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*) are abandoned by means of the door of liberation that is wishless; the yoke of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*) is abandoned by means of emptiness; and the yoke of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*) is abandoned by means of the signless.

Therein, the bodily tie of covetousness and the bodily tie of ill will reach abandonment through the door of liberation that is the wishless; the bodily tie of clinging to precepts and observances reaches abandonment through emptiness; and the bodily tie of adherence to "this is the truth" reaches abandonment through the signless.

Therein, the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence reach abandonment through the door of liberation that is the wishless; the taint of views reaches abandonment through emptiness; and the taint of ignorance reaches abandonment through the signless.

Therein, the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) reach their abandonment through the door of liberation that is wishless (*appaṇihita*); the flood of views (*diṭṭhi-ogha*) through emptiness (*suññatā*); and the flood of ignorance (*avijjā-ogha*) through the signless (*animitta*).

Therein, the dart of lust (*rāga-salla*) and the dart of hatred (*dosa-salla*) reach their abandonment through the door of liberation that is wishless; the dart of conceit (*māna-salla*) through emptiness; and the dart of delusion (*moha-salla*) through the signless.

Therein, the station of consciousness associated with form (*rūpūpaga-viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) and the station of consciousness associated with feeling (*vedanūpaga-viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) reach full understanding (*pariññā*) through the door of liberation that is wishless; [the station of consciousness] associated with perception (*saññūpaga*) through emptiness; and [the station of consciousness] associated with volitional formations (*saṅkhārūpaga*) through the signless.
Therein, going astray through desire and going astray through hatred are abandoned by means of the door of liberation that is the wishless;
going astray through fear is abandoned by means of emptiness; and going astray through delusion is abandoned by means of the door of liberation that is the signless.
Thus, all phenomena that follow the worldly cycle are led out.
Those worlds [are reached] by way of the three doors to liberation.
Herein, this is the outlet:
the four modes of practice, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four jhānas, the four abidings, the four...
The right efforts, the four wonderful and marvelous qualities, the four foundations, the four developments of concentration, the four qualities conducive to happiness, and the four immeasurables.

The first way of practice is the first foundation of mindfulness; the second way of practice is the second foundation of mindfulness; the third way of practice is the third foundation of mindfulness; the fourth way of practice is the fourth foundation of mindfulness.

The first foundation of mindfulness is the first jhāna; the second foundation of mindfulness is the second jhāna; the third foundation of mindfulness is the third jhāna; the fourth foundation of mindfulness is the fourth jhāna.
The first jhāna is the first abiding; the second jhāna is the second abiding; the third jhāna is the third abiding; the fourth jhāna is the fourth abiding.
The first abiding is the first right effort; the second abiding is the second right effort; the third abiding is the third right effort; the fourth abiding is the fourth right effort.
The first right effort is the first wonderful and marvelous quality; the second is the second; the third is the third; the fourth right effort is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality.
The first wonderful and marvelous quality is the first foundation; the second wonderful and marvelous quality...
The second foundation is the third wonderful and marvelous quality; the third foundation is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality.

The first foundation is the first development of concentration; the second foundation is the second development of concentration; the third foundation is the third development of concentration; the fourth foundation is the fourth development of concentration.
The first development of concentration is the first state partaking of happiness; the second development of concentration is the second state partaking of happiness;
the third development of concentration is the third state partaking of happiness; the fourth development of concentration is the fourth state partaking of happiness.
The first phenomenon conducive to happiness is the first immeasurable; the second phenomenon conducive to happiness is the second immeasurable;
the third phenomenon conducive to happiness is the third immeasurable; the fourth phenomenon conducive to happiness is the fourth immeasurable.
The first way of practice, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness;

the second way of practice, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the second foundation of mindfulness; the third way of practice, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the third foundation of mindfulness;
the fourth way of practice, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the fourth [foundation of mindfulness].
One fulfills the foundation of mindfulness.
The first foundation of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first jhāna;
the second foundation of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the second jhāna; the third foundation of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated...
It fulfills the third jhāna; the fourth foundation of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the fourth jhāna.
The first jhāna, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the first abiding;
the second jhāna, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the second abiding; the third jhāna, when developed and cultivated...
It fulfills the third abiding. The fourth jhāna, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the fourth abiding.
The first abiding, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
the second abiding, when developed and cultivated, [fulfills the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states...]
It fulfills abandonment; the third abiding, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
the fourth abiding, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the stability, non-confusion, and further increase of wholesome states that have already arisen.
The first right effort, developed and cultivated, fulfills the abandoning of conceit;
the second right effort, developed and cultivated, fulfills the uprooting of attachment;
the third right effort, developed and cultivated, fulfills the abandoning of ignorance; the fourth right effort, developed and cultivated...
It fulfills the subsiding of existence.
The abandoning of conceit, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the foundation of truth; the uprooting of attachment, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the foundation of relinquishment;
the abandoning of ignorance, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the foundation of wisdom.
It fulfills [the concentration of purpose]. The subsiding of existence, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the foundation of subsiding.
The foundation of truth, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the concentration of desire. The foundation of relinquishment, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the concentration of energy.
The foundation of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the concentration of mind.
It fulfills it; the foundation of concentration on tranquility, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the concentration on investigation.
Concentration through desire, when developed and cultivated, fulfills restraint of the faculties;
concentration through energy, when developed and cultivated, fulfills austerity; concentration through the mind, when developed and cultivated, fulfills wisdom.
Concentration through investigation, when developed and cultivated extensively, fulfills the relinquishment of all acquisitions.
Restraint of the sense faculties, when developed and cultivated extensively, fulfills loving-kindness. Austerity, when developed and cultivated extensively, fulfills compassion.
Intelligence, when developed and cultivated extensively, fulfills sympathetic joy. The relinquishment of all acquisitions...
When developed and cultivated extensively, it fulfills equanimity. In this regard,
these four directions constitute the first way of practice, the first foundation of mindfulness,
the first jhāna, the first abiding, the first right effort, the first wonderful and marvelous phenomenon, the resolution upon truth, and concentration through desire.
Restraint of the sense faculties and loving-kindness (*mettā*) are the first direction.

The second way of practice, the second foundation of mindfulness, the second jhāna, the second abiding, the second right effort, the second wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of energy, concentration through vigor, austerity, and compassion—these are the second direction.

The third way of practice, the third foundation of mindfulness, the third jhāna, the third abiding, the third right effort, the third wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of wisdom, concentration of mind, intelligence, and sympathetic joy (*muditā*)—these are the third direction.
The fourth way of practice, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, the fourth jhāna, the fourth abiding, the fourth right exertion,
the fourth wonderful and marvelous phenomenon, the basis of tranquility, the concentration of investigation,
the relinquishment of all acquisitions, and equanimity— this is the fourth direction.
In this regard, the first way of practice, the first foundation of mindfulness, the first jhāna, the first abiding, the first right effort,
the first wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of truth, concentration through desire,
restraint of the faculties, and loving-kindness— these ten suttas have one meaning; only the phrasing is different.
This is the medicine for a person of lustful temperament.
The second way of practice, the second foundation of mindfulness, the second jhāna, the second abiding, the second right effort,
the second wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of relinquishment, energy, concentration, austerity, and compassion— of these...
These ten suttas have a single meaning; only the phrasing is different.
This is the medicine for a person of a temperament characterized by hatred.
It is the third way of practice, the third foundation of mindfulness, the third jhāna, the third abiding, and the third right exertion.
The third wonderful and marvelous quality—wisdom as the foundation, concentration of mind, intelligence, and gladness—these ten discourses have one single meaning; only the phrasing differs.
This is the medicine for one of dull temperament who is dominated by views.
The fourth way of practice, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, the fourth jhāna, the fourth abiding, the fourth right effort,
the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality, the basis of serenity, the concentration of inquiry,
the relinquishment of all acquisitions, and equanimity— these ten suttas have one meaning; only the phrasing is different.
This is the medicine for one of speculative temperament who is exalted.
Therein, the painful practice with slow direct knowledge and the painful practice with quick direct knowledge are the door to liberation of the wishless;
the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge is the door to liberation of the void; the pleasant practice with... [quick direct knowledge is the door to liberation of the signless].
The signless liberation door is one of swift direct knowledge.

Therein, mindfulness-establishment consisting of contemplating the body in the body and mindfulness-establishment consisting of contemplating feelings in feelings are the wishless liberation door; mindfulness-establishment consisting of contemplating the mind in the mind is the emptiness liberation door;
and mindfulness-establishment consisting of contemplating phenomena in phenomena is the signless liberation door.
Therein, the first and second jhānas are the wishless gate to liberation; the third jhāna is the emptiness gate to liberation; the fourth jhāna is the signless gate to liberation.
Therein, the first and second abidings are the wishless gate to liberation; the third abiding is the emptiness gate to liberation; the fourth abiding is the signless gate to liberation.
Wherein the first and second right endeavors are the wishless gate to liberation.
The third right effort is the gate of liberation that is emptiness; the fourth right effort is the gate of liberation that is the signless.

Therein, the abandoning of conceit and the uprooting of attachment is the gate of liberation that is the desireless; the abandoning of ignorance is the gate of liberation that is emptiness; the stilling of becoming is the gate of liberation that is the signless.

Therein, the foundation of truth and the foundation of relinquishment are the gate of liberation that is the desireless; the foundation of wisdom is the gate of liberation that is emptiness; the foundation of peace is the gate of liberation that is the signless.

Therein, concentration through desire and concentration through energy are the wishless gateway to liberation; concentration through mind is the emptiness gateway to liberation; and concentration through investigation is the signless gateway to liberation.

Therein, restraint of the faculties and austerity are the wishless gateway to liberation; discernment is the emptiness gateway to liberation; and the relinquishment of all acquisitions is the signless gateway to liberation.
Therein, loving-kindness and compassion are the wishless gateway to liberation; sympathetic joy is the emptiness gateway to liberation; equanimity is the signless gateway to liberation.
These are their sport.
The four nutriments are their opposites, as are the four modes of practice... [and so on].
The four perversions have as their antidote the four foundations of mindfulness.
The four clingings have as their antidote the four jhānas.
The four yokes have as their antidote the four abidings.
There are four fetters; their antidote is the four right endeavors.
There are four taints; their antidote is the four wonderful and marvelous qualities.
There are four floods; their antidote is the four foundations.
There are four arrows; their opposite is the fourfold development of concentration.
There are four stations of consciousness; their opposite is the four states conducive to happiness.
There are four ways of going to ruin; their opposite is the four immeasurables.
The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples have destroyed lust, hatred, and delusion; their sport consists of development, realization, and the bringing of an end [to defilements].
Their sport is based on the faculties (*indriya*), and their sport is not based on perversions (*vipariyāsa*).
The faculties have the true Dhamma as their domain, while perversions have the defilements as their domain.
This is called the ground of the method of the lion’s sport and the method of the surveying of directions.
Therefore he said: “He who leads [beings] away from defilement by means of the perversions.
For in the analytical expositions (veyyākaraṇa), those things which are called “wholesome and unwholesome,” and so forth...

In this regard, those who emerge by means of the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge and those who emerge by means of the painful practice with swift direct knowledge—these are two types of persons.
Those who emerge by means of the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge and those who emerge by means of the pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge—these are two types of persons.
For these four types of persons, there is this corruption: the four nutriments, the four perversions, and the four...
The clingings, the four bonds, the four ties, the four taints,
the four floods, the four arrows, the four stations of consciousness, and the four ways of going to ruin—
this is the purification for those four types of persons: the four practices, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the four [bases of power].
The meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the four abidings (*vihāra*), the four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the four wonderful and marvelous qualities (*acchariya abbhuta dhamma*),

the four foundations (*adhiṭṭhāna*), the four developments of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*), the four qualities conducive to happiness (*sukhabhāgiya dhamma*), and the four immeasurables (*appamāṇa*). Among these,
those who emerge by means of the painful way with sluggish direct knowledge and the painful way with swift direct knowledge are these two types of persons.
There are two types of persons who proceed by way of the pleasant practice, namely, that with sluggish direct knowledge and that with swift direct knowledge.
Among them, the one who proceeds by way of the pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge is one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
The one who proceeds by way of the common [practice] is one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*).
One who is led out by a painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge is a person to be guided (*neyya*).

In this regard, the Blessed One teaches serenity (*samatha*) to the person who understands through a condensed instruction (*ugghaṭitaññu*), insight (*vipassanā*) to the person to be guided, and both serenity and insight to the person who understands through elaboration (*vipañcitaññu*).
In this regard, the Blessed One teaches a gentle Dharma-discourse to the person who understands through a condensed instruction, and a sharp [discourse] to...

For one who needs to be led, [the teaching] is slow and gentle; for one who understands through elaboration, it is detailed. In this regard, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma in brief to the person who understands through a condensed statement;
he teaches it both in brief and in detail to the person who understands through elaboration; and he teaches it in detail to the person who needs to be led.

In this regard, the Blessed One points out the escape to the person who understands through a condensed statement; he points out both the danger and the escape to the person who understands through elaboration; and he points out the gratification, the danger, and the escape to the person who needs to be led.

In that regard, the Blessed One prescribes the training in higher wisdom for one who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching, the training in higher mind for one who gains knowledge through an expanded teaching, and the training in higher virtue for one who is to be led.
Among these, there are two types of persons who emerge by means of the painful way with sluggish direct knowledge and the painful way with swift direct knowledge;
and those who emerge by means of the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge and the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge.
These are two persons.
Thus, having been four, they become three: the one who understands through a condensed statement, the one who understands through an elaboration, and the one who is led along.

For these three persons, this is the defilement: the three unwholesome roots—the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion—and the three types of misconduct.
Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind;
the three unwholesome thoughts:
sensual thought, ill-will thought, and cruelty thought.
Three unwholesome perceptions:
the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of cruelty;
three inverted perceptions:
The perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, and the perception of self;
the three feelings— the pleasant feeling, the painful feeling, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Three kinds of suffering:
the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change;
three fires:
The fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion;
the three arrows— the arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, and the arrow of delusion.
Three tangles:
the tangle of lust, the tangle of hatred, and the tangle of delusion;
three unwholesome investigations:
Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and unwholesome mental action.
There are three failures:
failure in virtue, failure in view, and failure in conduct.
For these three persons, this is the purification:
the three roots of the wholesome—
non-greed as a root of the wholesome, non-hatred as a root of the wholesome, and non-delusion as a root of the wholesome.
The three types of good conduct:
good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
The three types of wholesome thoughts:
The thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-cruelty.
Three kinds of concentration:

concentration with applied thought and sustained thought, concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Three wholesome perceptions:
the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, and the perception of non-cruelty.
Three unperverted perceptions:
The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, and the perception of non-self.
Three wholesome investigations:
wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action, and wholesome mental action.
Three purities:
purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind;
three successes:
The perfection of virtue, the perfection of concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
The three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
Three aggregates:
the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.
Three gateways to liberation:
"Emptiness, the signless, and the desireless.
Thus, having been four, they become three; having been three, they become two: the one of craving-temperament and the one of view-temperament.
For these two types of persons, this is the defilement: craving, ignorance, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread.
Lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension, improper attention, laziness, difficult-to-correctness,
the conceit "I am," the conceit "mine," lack of faith, negligence, not hearing the true Dharma, lack of restraint, covetousness, ill will,
the hindrances, the fetters, anger, resentment, contempt, domineering, envy, and avarice.
Deceit, guile, the view of eternalism, and the view of annihilationism—
these are the stains for these two types of persons. Their purification consists of serenity and insight, moral shame and moral dread, mindfulness and clear comprehension,
wise attention, the arousal of energy, readiness to listen, and knowledge of the Dhamma.
Knowledge of the sequence, knowledge of destruction, and knowledge of non-arising; faith and diligence; hearing the true Dhamma and restraint;
non-covetousness and non-ill will; liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, and liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance;
clear realization; fewness of desires and contentment; absence of anger and absence of malice; absence of disparagement and absence of domineering.
And the abandoning of envy, the abandoning of stinginess, true knowledge, liberation, liberation with a conditioned object,
liberation with an unconditioned object, the element of nirvana with residue remaining, and the element of nirvana without residue remaining—
this is called the plane of the Tipukkhalo method and the Aṅkuso method.
Therefore it was said: "He who leads [the mind] away from the unwholesome together with its roots," and "having looked with the eye of vision.
This concludes the section on the origin of the method.
